DIGITAL ASSETS AND ONLINE ACCOUNT ACCESS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan T. Reyes · Pat M. Alvarez

PURPOSE OF THIS DIGITAL ASSETS AND ONLINE ACCOUNT ACCESS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (Probate Code sections 870 through 884), the statutory framework governing when and how a fiduciary — an executor or other personal representative, a trustee, an agent acting under a power of attorney, or a conservator — may obtain access to a person's digital assets and online accounts from the company or platform that holds them (the “custodian”), such as an email provider, a social media platform, or a cloud storage service. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning the digital assets and online accounts of Pat M. Alvarez, in connection with Jordan T. Reyes's prospective or actual role as Personal representative (executor). This statutory framework operates alongside — not in place of — the general authority a will, trust, or power of attorney already grants a fiduciary over a person's property; it supplies the specific rules a custodian and a fiduciary must follow for digital assets and online accounts specifically, including what document a fiduciary must produce, how and when a custodian must respond, and the different rules that apply depending on whether the fiduciary is asking for the content of a user's electronic communications (such as the text of emails or messages) or only a catalogue of them (such as sender, recipient, and timestamp information without message content). This information sheet does not itself grant Jordan T. Reyes access to any digital asset or online account belonging to Pat M. Alvarez, does not itself constitute the will, trust, power of attorney, court order, or other record a custodian may require, and does not determine what any specific custodian will disclose in any specific case.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: “DIGITAL ASSET,” “CUSTODIAN,” AND THE CONTENT/CATALOGUE DISTINCTION
California's Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act defines the terms that determine what it reaches and how. A “digital asset” is defined broadly: “Digital asset” means an electronic record in which an individual has a right or interest. — meaning the term covers essentially any electronic record a person has a right or interest in, not a fixed list of specific account types, though the statute separately clarifies that an underlying asset or liability isn't itself a “digital asset” merely because it is recorded electronically, unless that asset or liability is itself an electronic record. The “custodian” is the company or platform on the other side of the relationship: “Custodian” means a person who carries, maintains, processes, receives, or stores a digital asset of a user. — for example, an email provider, a social media platform, or a cloud storage service holding Pat M. Alvarez's account. The Act also draws a sharp line between two kinds of information a custodian might disclose about an account. A “catalogue of electronic communications” is limited to envelope-level information: “Catalogue of electronic communications” means information that identifies each person with which a user has had an electronic communication, the time and date of the communication, and the electronic address of the person.. “Content of an electronic communication,” by contrast, reaches the substance of what was actually said: “Content of an electronic communication” means information concerning the substance or meaning of the communication, which meets all of the following requirements:(1) Has been sent or received by a user.(2) Is in electronic storage by a custodian providing an electronic communication service to the public or is carried or maintained by a custodian providing a remote-computing service to the public.(3) Is not readily accessible to the public. As the clauses below describe, which document a fiduciary must produce, and how specifically a will, trust, or power of attorney must address digital assets, differs depending on whether a fiduciary is requesting a catalogue or content.

Most states have enacted some version of the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, but the details — including document requirements, timeframes, and liability protections — can differ from state to state, and this document describes California's version only. This clause cites four subsections of the same statutory section, § 871(c), (d), (f), and (h); they are treated here as one source describing that one section's definitions, not as four independent corroborating sources. One correction to an initial research assumption: the content-versus-catalogue distinction is defined here, in § 871(c) and (d), but the specific document requirements that turn on that distinction appear in later, separate sections (§§ 876-877 for a personal representative, §§ 878-879 for a trustee, and §§ 879.1-879.2 for an agent) rather than in § 875, which instead concerns a custodian's own discretion over the degree and format of access it grants and permits a reasonable administrative charge for disclosure — not the content/catalogue split itself. No published California case law interpreting these definitions was located or relied on for this document; it is based on the statutory text alone. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself grant any fiduciary access to any digital asset or online account, does not itself constitute the will, trust, power of attorney, court order, or other record a custodian may require, and does not determine what any specific custodian will provide, require, or accept in response to any specific request.

WHICH FIDUCIARIES, TIME PERIODS, AND ACCOUNTS THIS ACT COVERS
The Act applies broadly across fiduciary roles and across time: (a) This part shall apply to all of the following:(1) A fiduciary acting under a will executed before, on, or after January 1, 2017.(2) A personal representative acting for a decedent who died before, on, or after January 1, 2017.(3) A trustee acting under a trust created before, on, or after January 1, 2017.(4) A custodian of digital assets for a user if the user resides in this state or resided in this state at the time of the user’s death.(5) A conservator appointed before, on, or after January 1, 2025.(6) A fiduciary acting under a power of attorney executed before, on, or after January 1, 2025. Read together, this reaches a fiduciary acting under a will, a personal representative administering a decedent's estate, a trustee, a conservator, and — as of a 2024 amendment effective January 1, 2025 — an agent acting under a power of attorney, regardless of when the underlying document was executed or the relevant appointment made, and regardless of whether Pat M. Alvarez's account predates the statute. It also reaches any custodian of digital assets for a user who resides, or resided at death, in California. The Act carves out one category from its coverage entirely: (b) This part does not apply to a digital asset of an employer used by an employee in the ordinary course of the employer’s business. — meaning a workplace email or file-storage account Pat M. Alvarez used only in the ordinary course of an employer's business is not covered by this framework at all, whatever role Jordan T. Reyes holds.

THE THREE-TIER PRIORITY SYSTEM: ONLINE TOOL, THEN ESTATE-PLANNING DOCUMENT, THEN TERMS OF SERVICE
The Act establishes a specific order of priority for who controls disclosure of a user's digital assets. First, a custodian-provided online tool controls if the user used one: (a) A user may use an online tool to direct the custodian to disclose to a designated recipient or not disclose some or all of the user’s digital assets, including the content of electronic communications. If the online tool allows the user to modify or delete a direction at all times, a direction regarding disclosure using an online tool overrides a contrary direction by the user in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record. — meaning a service like an account's own built-in legacy-contact or inactive-account-management feature, where one exists and Pat M. Alvarez used it to give a direction that could be changed or deleted at any time, overrides anything Pat M. Alvarez said in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record. Second, only if Pat M. Alvarez did not use such a tool, or the custodian never offered one, does a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record control: (b) If a user has not used an online tool to give direction under subdivision (a) or if a custodian has not provided an online tool, a user may allow or prohibit in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record the disclosure to a fiduciary of some or all of the user’s digital assets, including the contents of electronic communications sent or received by the user. Third, absent both of the above, the custodian's own terms-of-service agreement governs by default: (c) A fiduciary’s or designated recipient’s access to digital assets may be modified or eliminated by a user, by federal law, or by a terms-of-service agreement when the user has not provided any direction that is recognized in Section 873. — meaning where Pat M. Alvarez used no online tool and left no direction in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record, Jordan T. Reyes's access to a given account depends on whatever the custodian's own terms of service, or federal law, otherwise allow.

WHAT A PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE MUST GIVE A CUSTODIAN — AND WHY CONTENT REQUIRES MORE THAN A CATALOGUE DOES
Where Jordan T. Reyes acts as personal representative of Pat M. Alvarez's estate, the Act sets different requirements depending on whether the request is for content or only a catalogue. To obtain the catalogue of a deceased user's electronic communications, and any digital assets other than content, a personal representative generally need only establish the standard facts of the appointment: Unless the user prohibited disclosure of digital assets or the court directs otherwise, a custodian shall disclose to the personal representative of the estate of a deceased user a catalogue of electronic communications sent or received by the user and digital assets, other than the content of electronic communications, of the user, if the personal representative gives to the custodian all of the following:(a) A written request for disclosure in physical or electronic form.(b) A certified copy of the death certificate of the user.(c) A certified copy of the letter of appointment of the representative, a small-estate affidavit under Section 13101, or court order. To obtain the content of a deceased user's electronic communications instead, the Act requires the same threshold documents plus something more specific: If a deceased user consented to or a court directs disclosure of the content of electronic communications of the user, the custodian shall disclose to the personal representative of the estate of the user the content of an electronic communication sent or received by the user if the personal representative gives to the custodian all of the following: (d) Unless the user provided direction using an online tool, a copy of the user’s will, trust, power of attorney, or other record evidencing the user’s consent to disclosure of the content of electronic communications. In other words, a document that generally authorizes a personal representative to administer an estate is enough by itself for the catalogue tier, but obtaining actual message content requires a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record that specifically evidences Pat M. Alvarez's consent to disclosure of content — not merely a general grant of estate-administration authority. The content provision also lets a custodian, before disclosing, require a court finding that disclosure would not violate the federal Stored Communications Act (18 U.S.C. § 2701 et seq.) — a reminder that this state statute operates alongside, and does not override, that separate federal constraint on a custodian's disclosure of communications content.

WHAT A TRUSTEE MUST GIVE A CUSTODIAN — THE SAME CONTENT/CATALOGUE SPLIT, TIED TO THE SETTLOR'S CONSENT
The Act imposes a parallel structure on a trustee seeking digital assets held in a trust's account, again splitting catalogue from content. For the catalogue of electronic communications sent or received through the trust's account, and other digital assets short of content, a trustee generally need only certify its status and the settlor's death: a custodian shall disclose, to a trustee that is not an original user of an account, the catalogue of electronic communications sent or received by an original or successor user and stored, carried, or maintained by the custodian in an account of the trust and any digital assets, other than the content of electronic communications, in which the trust has a right or interest if the settlor of the trust is deceased and the trustee gives the custodian all of the following:(a) A written request for disclosure in physical or electronic form.(b) A certified copy of the death certificate of the settlor.(c) A certified copy of the trust instrument or a certification of trust under Section 18100.5. For content, the Act again requires something beyond the trustee's basic authority: a custodian shall disclose to a trustee that is not an original user of an account the content of an electronic communication sent or received by an original or successor user and carried, maintained, processed, received, or stored by the custodian in the account of the trust if the trustee gives to the custodian all of the following: (c) A certified copy of the trust instrument, or a certification of trust under Section 18100.5, evidencing the settlor’s consent to disclosure of the content of electronic communications to the trustee. As with a personal representative, a trust instrument that generally names Jordan T. Reyes as trustee and describes ordinary trustee powers is not, by its terms, described by the statute as sufficient for content; the trust instrument or certification of trust must evidence the settlor's consent to disclosure of content specifically.

WHAT AN AGENT UNDER A POWER OF ATTORNEY MUST GIVE A CUSTODIAN — CONTENT REQUIRES AN EXPRESS GRANT
For an agent acting under a power of attorney — a role this Act only reached starting with a 2024 amendment effective January 1, 2025 — the statute states its general-versus-specific requirement more explicitly than it does for a personal representative or trustee. For the catalogue of a principal's electronic communications and non-content digital assets, either a specific or a general grant of authority in the power of attorney is enough: a custodian shall disclose to an agent with specific authority over digital assets or general authority to act on behalf of a principal a catalogue of electronic communications sent or received by the principal and digital assets, other than the content of electronic communications, of the principal if the agent gives the custodian all of the following: (a) A written request for disclosure in physical or electronic form. (b) An original or copy of the power of attorney that gives the agent specific authority over digital assets or general authority to act on behalf of the principal. For content, the statute requires more: To the extent a power of attorney expressly grants an agent authority over the content of electronic communications sent or received by the principal, and unless directed otherwise by the principal or the court, a custodian shall disclose the content of electronic communications to the agent if the agent gives the custodian all of the following: (a) A written request for disclosure in physical or electronic form. (b) An original or copy of the power of attorney expressly granting the agent authority over the content of electronic communications of the principal. Unlike the catalogue tier, the power of attorney must expressly grant Jordan T. Reyes authority over content specifically; a power of attorney that only grants an agent general authority to act on Pat M. Alvarez's behalf, without expressly addressing the content of electronic communications, does not by its terms satisfy this requirement, even though that same general grant is enough for the catalogue tier.

THE CUSTODIAN'S 60-DAY RESPONSE DEADLINE, AND THE GOOD-FAITH LIABILITY SHIELD
Once a fiduciary or designated recipient has given a custodian the information the Act requires, the custodian is on a statutory clock: (a) Not later than 60 days after receipt of the information required under Sections 876 to 879.3, inclusive, a custodian shall comply with a request under this part from a fiduciary or designated recipient to disclose digital assets or terminate an account. If the custodian fails to comply with a request, the fiduciary or designated recipient may apply to the court for an order directing compliance. The Act also protects a custodian that complies: (f) (1) A custodian and its officers, employees, and agents are immune from liability for an act or omission done in good faith and in compliance with this part.(2) The protections specified in paragraph (1) do not apply in a case of gross negligence or willful or wanton misconduct of the custodian or its officers, employees, or agents. — meaning a custodian that discloses digital assets, or declines to, in a good-faith, compliant response to a request under this Act is shielded from liability for that act or omission, except where the custodian or its officers, employees, or agents acted with gross negligence or willful or wanton misconduct. A custodian is not without options if it questions a request: the same section lets a custodian require a fiduciary or designated recipient to first obtain a court order making specific findings, including that the account belongs to the decedent, principal, conservatee, or trustee in question, and that compliance would not violate the federal Stored Communications Act (18 U.S.C. § 2702) — another point at which this state statute is written to operate alongside, not in place of, that separate federal constraint.

Alvarez, does not itself constitute the will, trust, power of attorney, court order, or other record a custodian may require, and does not determine what any specific custodian will disclose in any specific case.

California's Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act defines the terms that determine what it reaches and how. A “digital asset” is defined broadly: “Digital asset” means an electronic record in which an individual has a right or interest. — meaning the term covers essentially any electronic record a person has a right or interest in, not a fixed list of specific account types, though the statute separately clarifies that an underlying asset or liability isn't itself a “digital asset” merely because it is recorded electronically, unless that asset or liability is itself an electronic record. The “custodian” is the company or platform on the other side of the relationship: “Custodian” means a person who carries, maintains, processes, receives, or stores a digital asset of a user. — for example, an email provider, a social media platform, or a cloud storage service holding Pat M. Alvarez's account. The Act also draws a sharp line between two kinds of information a custodian might disclose about an account. A “catalogue of electronic communications” is limited to envelope-level information: “Catalogue of electronic communications” means information that identifies each person with which a user has had an electronic communication, the time and date of the communication, and the electronic address of the person.. “Content of an electronic communication,” by contrast, reaches the substance of what was actually said: “Content of an electronic communication” means information concerning the substance or meaning of the communication, which meets all of the following requirements:(1) Has been sent or received by a user.(2) Is in electronic storage by a custodian providing an electronic communication service to the public or is carried or maintained by a custodian providing a remote-computing service to the public.(3) Is not readily accessible to the public. citations.quote: (f) (1) A custodian and its officers, employees, and agents are immune from liability for an act or omission done in good faith and in compliance with this part.(2) The protections specified in paragraph (1) do not apply in a case of gross negligence or willful or wanton misconduct of the custodian or its officers, employees, or agents.

expectedJSON.gap: This is California's own statute, used here as real evidence of what California's Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act actually provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific fiduciary's access to any specific account. Most states have enacted some version of the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, but the details — including document requirements, timeframes, and liability protections — can differ from state to state, and this document describes California's version only. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 881(a) and (f); they are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. This confirms the assumption in the original research brief that the statute sets both a specific response timeframe and a liability protection for a compliant custodian; the 60-day period runs from the custodian's receipt of the information required by the specific disclosure section that applies to that fiduciary's role (§§ 876 through 879.3), and the immunity is qualified — it does not extend to a custodian's gross negligence or willful or wanton misconduct. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself grant any fiduciary access to any digital asset or online account, does not itself constitute the will, trust, power of attorney, court order, or other record a custodian may require, and does not determine what any specific custodian will provide, require, or accept in response to any specific request.
